questions.prompt: What makes the Nuna chapter a commitment case in this book?
choices: It shows commitment as a company story about staying bound to chosen priorities
It argues that priorities matter only when they are easy
It replaces buy-in with silence and obedience

explanation.gentle: The chapter moves commitment out of theory and into a company case.
explanation.direct: Its main job is to show how chosen priorities gain force only when people stay bound to them.
explanation.competitive: This case is about carrying the choice, not just admiring it.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter distinguish commitment from awareness?
choices: Awareness is costly while commitment is effortless
Commitment begins when chosen priorities govern calendars, tradeoffs, and effort
Awareness means the priority was badly chosen

explanation.gentle: People can agree with a priority before they actually carry it.
explanation.direct: The chapter says commitment starts when behavior answers to the priority.
explanation.competitive: Reciting the priority is cheap; obeying it in the calendar is not.

questions.prompt: Why is forced compliance a weak substitute for commitment in this chapter?
choices: Because the chapter rejects any form of structure
Because pressure can imitate order without creating real buy-in
Because commitment requires zero tradeoffs

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps buy-in separate from pressured obedience.
explanation.direct: Coercion can copy the surface pattern without the inner transfer of burden.
explanation.competitive: Fear can stage commitment and still fail to make it real.

questions.prompt: Leila sees a lab leadership team praise a new priority while the old reporting work still owns the week. What best fits the chapter?
choices: The team is committed because everyone agreed in the meeting
The team is wisely keeping all options open
The team has not yet shown commitment because the old obligations still govern behavior

explanation.gentle: Agreement is weaker than the behavioral change the chapter demands.
explanation.direct: If the calendar still serves the old stack, the chosen priority lacks real authority.
explanation.competitive: A meeting win means nothing if the old regime still runs the week.

questions.prompt: A student nonprofit board keeps talking about one main initiative but never removes older projects from its calendar. What chapter failure does this show?
choices: Decorative commitment created by agreement without carried burden
Healthy backup planning
Proof that the board is committed to every priority equally

explanation.gentle: The board kept the language of commitment without the cost that proves it.
explanation.direct: Old projects kept their privileges, so the new initiative never truly governed.
explanation.competitive: They wanted the credit for commitment without paying the price.

questions.prompt: Which reading does the chapter reject as a misreading of commitment?
choices: Commitment means obedience alone
Commitment changes what a team postpones and protects
Commitment makes priorities govern action

explanation.gentle: The chapter says commitment is more than outward submission.
explanation.direct: Obedience theater can look disciplined while still lacking buy-in.
explanation.competitive: If pressure is your whole explanation, you missed the chapter.

questions.prompt: What is happening when old obligations still control the calendar after a new priority is announced?
choices: Hedging is draining force from the chosen work
The team has already proven durable commitment
The chapter says calendars do not matter

explanation.gentle: Hedging lets the old stack stay alive under the new words.
explanation.direct: The chapter uses this mismatch to explain decorative OKRs.
explanation.competitive: If the leftovers still rule the calendar, the new priority is mostly branded intent.

questions.prompt: A team sounds symbolically united but cannot name what work lost protection for the new priority. Which judgment best fits the chapter?
choices: The team has strong buy-in because nobody objected
The team may have symbolic agreement but not real carried commitment
The team should avoid asking what changed

explanation.gentle: Real commitment normally leaves some visible displacement behind it.
explanation.direct: If nothing lost status, the unity may be symbolic instead of operational.
explanation.competitive: Harmony without sacrifice is usually a warning sign here.

questions.prompt: What deeper point does the chapter make about decorative OKRs?
choices: They are priorities that remain visible in language while lacking governing power in behavior
They are useful backups for when teams get tired
They disappear because the company stopped talking about priorities

explanation.gentle: The problem is not absence of priorities but weakness of control.
explanation.direct: Decorative OKRs stay present on the slide while the older stack still governs action.
explanation.competitive: They look official because they were never meant to win real authority.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 6 naturally lead into an alignment chapter next?
choices: Because commitment removes the need for coordination
Because once one team is truly bound to priorities, the next challenge is how multiple committed teams connect
Because company cases end after commitment

explanation.gentle: The bridge asks how committed teams move together.
explanation.direct: After commitment makes priorities real inside one team, alignment becomes the next issue.
explanation.competitive: Once the load is real, coordination becomes the fight.
